title: Patient acceptance of continuous wearable vital-sign monitoring on surgical wards: A prospective mixed-methods survey study
content:
by Ephrahim E. Jerry, Daphne L. J. Nabben, Ashley J. R. De Bie Dekker, Igor W. F. Paulussen, R. Arthur Bouwman, Simon W. Nienhuijs

Background

Continuous wearable monitoring of vital signs is increasingly implemented on hospital wards to enable early detection of clinical deterioration and to reduce the burden of intermittent vital-sign measurements. While feasibility of wearable monitoring and its acceptance among healthcare professionals have been demonstrated, patient perspectives remain underexplored.

Objective

To evaluate patient experiences with wearable monitoring devices during hospitalization.

Methods

This prospective, single-center mixed-methods study included adult surgical ward patients monitored with a wearable device (Healthdot or viQtor) for ≥ 24 hours. Patients completed 15 five-point Likert items assessing patient experience and a separate overall satisfaction rating on a 1–10 scale. Qualitative material comprised free-text responses from 36 of the 102 participants and two additional semistructured interviews with participants from the same cohort. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, exploratory monitoring-context comparisons, and multivariable regression. Qualitative data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s thematic-analysis approach.

Results

A total of 102 patients were included in the final analysis after exclusion of two duplicate questionnaire records. Mean overall acceptance was 4.05 ± 0.54 on a 1–5 scale (95% CI 3.94–4.15), and mean satisfaction was 8.21 ± 1.39 on a 1–10 scale (95% CI 7.93–8.48). Acceptance was higher in the Healthdot context than in the viQtor context, with an exploratory mean difference of 0.40 points (95% CI 0.18–0.62). Qualitative findings indicated generally limited burden, but also concerns regarding comfort and patient information.

Conclusions

Patients in this single-center cohort generally reported favorable experiences with continuous wearable vital-sign monitoring. Acceptance differed between the two monitoring contexts, but the study design does not allow these differences to be attributed to a causal effect of device type. Further studies should validate the questionnaire and evaluate clinical effectiveness, safety, cost-effectiveness, and longer-term implementation outcomes.
